column9: stem
column14: option_a
column15: option_b
column16: option_c
column17: option_d
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Which sentence best describes photosynthesis?
column14: Plants absorb ready-made food from the soil through their roots and store it in their leaves
column15: Plants and other producers use light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water
column16: Leaf cells divide to make new leaves
column17: Cells break down glucose and store the released energy in ATP
column28: Photosynthesis uses light energy to build glucose out of carbon dioxide and water, and it releases oxygen. Breaking down glucose to make ATP is cellular respiration, the process most often mixed up with photosynthesis. Roots take in water and minerals, not food.
column29: "Photo" means light and "synthesis" means putting something together.

column9: Photosynthesis changes light energy into ___ energy that is stored in sugar.
column28: Photosynthesis turns light energy into chemical energy, which is stored in the bonds of glucose. A common mistake is writing "heat" or "ATP"; ATP is a molecule, not a type of energy.
column29: Food and batteries both store this kind of energy in their molecules.

column9: Where does a land plant get most of the water it uses for photosynthesis?
column14: It pulls water out of the air through its bark
column15: It makes water from the sugar it stores
column16: Its roots absorb water from the soil
column17: Its flowers make the water
column28: Roots absorb water from the soil, and the water travels up the stem to the leaves. Flowers and bark do not supply water for photosynthesis, and a plant does not make its photosynthesis water from sugar.
column29: Think about where you pour the water when you water a houseplant.

column9: The word photosynthesis starts with "photo." What does "photo" refer to?
column14: Light
column15: Plants
column16: Sugar
column17: Water
column28: "Photo" means light, the energy source for photosynthesis. "Synthesis" means building something, the sugar. A common mistake is thinking "photo" means plant.
column29: A photograph is made by capturing this.

column9: Select every substance (matter) that a plant uses up as a reactant in photosynthesis. Select all that apply.
column14: Carbon dioxide
column15: Oxygen
column16: Water
column17: Glucose
column28: The reactants are carbon dioxide and water. Light supplies the energy but is not matter. Oxygen and glucose are products, not reactants, and nitrogen gas is not part of the reaction. Choosing oxygen is the most common mistake.
column29: Reactants go on the left side of the arrow in the photosynthesis equation.

column9: Select every product of photosynthesis. Select all that apply.
column14: Carbon dioxide
column15: Glucose
column16: Nitrogen gas
column17: Oxygen
column28: Photosynthesis makes glucose and oxygen. Carbon dioxide is a reactant that gets used up. Nitrogen gas and soil minerals are not made by photosynthesis. A common mistake is picking carbon dioxide because it is a product of cellular respiration.
column29: Products are what the reaction makes. Which of these does a plant give off or store?

column9: Leaves look green because of a green pigment called ___.
column28: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy. A common mistake is writing "chloroplast," which is the organelle that holds the chlorophyll, not the pigment itself.
column29: It starts with "chloro-," which means green.

column9: An organism such as a sunflower that makes its own food from light energy is called a(n) ___.
column28: An autotroph (also called a producer) makes its own food. Plants, algae, and some bacteria are autotrophs that use photosynthesis. A heterotroph has to eat other organisms for food, which is the common mix-up.
column29: "Auto" means self and "troph" means feeding.

column9: Why do most plant leaves look green to us?
column14: Chlorophyll absorbs green light better than any other color
column15: Green is the only color of light found in sunlight
column16: Leaves are filled with green-colored water
column17: Chlorophyll reflects most green light instead of absorbing it
column28: We see the colors that bounce off an object. Chlorophyll absorbs other colors well but reflects much of the green light, so leaves look green. The most common mistake is thinking leaves absorb green light best; it is the color they use least.
column29: The color you see is the color that bounces back to your eyes.

column9: In a maple tree, where does most photosynthesis take place?
column14: The bark of the trunk
column15: The roots
column16: The leaves
column17: The seeds
column28: Leaves are packed with chloroplasts and are spread out to catch sunlight, so most photosynthesis happens there. Roots are underground with no light, and bark and seeds have few or no chloroplasts.
column29: Which part of the tree is green and spread out to catch sunlight?

column9: Tiny openings on the underside of a leaf let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out. What are these openings called?
column14: Stomata
column15: Roots
column16: Thylakoids
column17: Veins
column28: Stomata (one is a stoma) are pores in the leaf surface for gas exchange. Veins carry water and sugar, and thylakoids are inside the chloroplast. A common mistake is choosing veins because they also move materials.
column29: The word comes from the Greek word for "mouth."

column9: Select every organism that carries out photosynthesis. Select all that apply.
column14: An oak tree
column15: A mushroom
column16: Green algae in a pond
column17: A white-tailed deer
column28: Oak trees, algae, cyanobacteria, and moss all have chlorophyll and make their own food. Mushrooms are fungi and deer are animals; they are heterotrophs. A common mistake is leaving out cyanobacteria because they are bacteria, but they do photosynthesis.
column29: Look for organisms that have chlorophyll and make their own food.

column9: During which stage of photosynthesis is light energy captured?
column14: The Calvin cycle
column15: The light-dependent reactions
column16: The Krebs cycle
column17: Glycolysis
column28: Light energy is captured in the light-dependent reactions. The Calvin cycle uses the energy afterward to build sugar. Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle are stages of cellular respiration, a common mix-up.
column29: One stage has the word "light" right in its name.

column9: Match each part of a chloroplast to its description.
column14: Thylakoid :: A flattened, disk-shaped sac inside the chloroplast
column15: Granum :: A stack of thylakoids, like a stack of coins
column16: Stroma :: The thick fluid that fills the chloroplast around the stacks
column17: Outer membrane :: The outer boundary that surrounds the whole chloroplast
column28: Thylakoids are the disks, a granum (plural grana) is a stack of them, the stroma is the fluid around the stacks, and the outer membrane surrounds everything. A common mistake is mixing up the stroma (fluid) with the stoma (a leaf pore).
column29: Start with the smallest part, the single disk, then find what a stack of them is called.

column9: Wisconsin maple syrup is made by boiling down sap that contains sugar. Where did that sugar first come from?
column14: Rainwater that soaked into the bark
column15: The bark makes sugar without any energy source
column16: Minerals the tree's roots took from the soil
column17: Photosynthesis in the maple's leaves
column28: The leaves made sugar by photosynthesis during the growing season, and the tree stored it (as starch) over the winter. In spring it moves through the sap. Soil and rain supply minerals and water, not sugar.
column29: Which part of the tree makes food using sunlight?

column9: A houseplant is left in a dark closet for three weeks while the family is on vacation. Why does it start to die?
column14: It cannot get carbon dioxide in a closet, because the door blocks the air
column15: Without light it cannot do photosynthesis, so it cannot make glucose
column16: Its roots grow too fast in the dark
column17: Closets have no oxygen, so the plant cannot do any cellular respiration
column28: Photosynthesis needs light energy. In the dark the plant keeps using stored sugar for cellular respiration but can't make more, so it runs out of food. Closets still have air with both carbon dioxide and oxygen.
column29: What does the closet take away that the plant needs to make food?

column9: What is the main sugar made by photosynthesis?
column14: ATP
column15: Carbon dioxide
column16: Glucose
column17: Protein
column28: Photosynthesis makes the sugar glucose. ATP is an energy carrier, not a sugar, carbon dioxide is a reactant, and protein is not a sugar. Picking ATP is the most common mistake.
column29: It is the same sugar your cells break down for energy.

column9: Which of these is a heterotroph that cannot carry out photosynthesis?
column14: Pond algae
column15: Duckweed
column16: Grass
column17: A cottontail rabbit
column28: A rabbit has no chloroplasts and must eat plants for food, so it is a heterotroph. Grass, algae, and duckweed (a tiny floating plant) are producers. A common mistake is thinking algae are animals because they live in water.
column29: Which one has to eat its food?

column9: Which stage of photosynthesis builds sugar molecules out of carbon dioxide?
column14: The Calvin cycle
column15: Glycolysis
column16: The light-dependent reactions
column17: Fermentation
column28: The Calvin cycle uses carbon dioxide and energy from the light-dependent reactions to build sugar. The light-dependent reactions capture light energy but don't make sugar. Glycolysis and fermentation break sugar down instead of building it.
column29: One stage captures energy; the other uses that energy to build.

column9: Bubbles rise from an elodea water plant sitting under a bright lamp. Which gas is in the bubbles?
column14: Nitrogen
column15: Carbon dioxide
column16: Oxygen
column17: Hydrogen
column28: Elodea releases oxygen as a product of photosynthesis, and it forms bubbles in the water. A common mistake is choosing carbon dioxide, which the plant takes in.
column29: Is the plant giving off a reactant or a product?

column9: The Calvin cycle is the stage of photosynthesis that releases oxygen gas.
column28: False. Oxygen is released during the light-dependent reactions in the thylakoids. The Calvin cycle uses carbon dioxide to build sugar and does not give off oxygen.
column29: Think about which stage uses the light energy and which stage builds sugar.

column9: Plant cells carry out cellular respiration as well as photosynthesis.
column28: True. Plant cells have mitochondria and break down glucose to make ATP all day and all night. Photosynthesis makes the glucose; respiration releases its energy. A common mistake is thinking plants do only photosynthesis.
column29: Plant cells need ATP too. Where does a cell's ATP come from?

column9: Carotenoids are yellow and orange pigments found in leaves. Why are they usually hidden during the summer?
column14: They are stored in the roots during summer
column15: Leaves contain much more chlorophyll, and its green color covers them up
column16: Carotenoids are only made after the first frost, when the nights turn cold
column17: Summer sunlight bleaches them white
column28: Carotenoids are in the leaf all summer, but there is far more chlorophyll, so the leaf looks green. In fall the chlorophyll breaks down and the yellows and oranges show. A common mistake is thinking fall colors are brand-new pigments.
column29: Two colors are in the same leaf. Which one is there in a much bigger amount?

column9: What is a pigment?
column14: A molecule that absorbs certain colors of light
column15: A tiny pore in a leaf
column16: An enzyme that builds sugar
column17: A kind of sugar stored in roots
column28: A pigment is a molecule that absorbs some colors of light and reflects others. Chlorophyll and carotenoids are pigments. A tiny leaf pore is a stoma, and an enzyme speeds up reactions.
column29: Paint and markers get their colors from these.

column9: In a food chain, why are plants at the very first level?
column14: They eat dead animals
column15: They are the smallest organisms in the chain, so everything else is able to eat them
column16: They eat the soil
column17: They capture energy from sunlight and store it in food that consumers eat
column28: Plants are producers: they capture light energy and store it as chemical energy in glucose. Every consumer in the chain gets its energy, directly or indirectly, from that food. Size has nothing to do with it, and plants don't eat soil.
column29: Where does the energy enter the food chain?

column9: Guard cells on a leaf's surface open and close tiny pores. On a hot, dry day they close the pores. What does this help the plant do?
column14: Absorb more light
column15: Save water
column16: Make more glucose
column17: Take in more carbon dioxide
column28: Closing the pores keeps water vapor from escaping, so the plant saves water. The trade-off is that less carbon dioxide can get in, so the plant makes less glucose, not more.
column29: What does a plant risk losing on a hot, dry day?

column9: Plants link many glucose molecules together to store them as ___, like the energy stored in a potato.
column28: Plants store extra glucose as starch, a long chain of glucose molecules. Potatoes, corn, and rice are full of it. A common mistake is writing cellulose, which is also made of glucose but builds cell walls instead of storing energy.
column29: It is the carbohydrate that turns iodine dark blue-black.

column9: Sunlight looks white. What is white sunlight actually made of?
column14: Only red light
column15: No colors at all
column16: A mix of all the colors of visible light
column17: Only green light
column28: White light is a mix of all the colors of the visible spectrum: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. A prism or a rainbow splits them apart. Pigments in leaves absorb some of those colors.
column29: Think about what a prism or a rainbow shows you.

column9: A lamp is moved closer to an elodea plant in a beaker of water. What will most likely happen to the number of bubbles it gives off each minute?
column14: It goes up
column15: It drops to zero
column16: It goes down
column17: The bubbles change into carbon dioxide
column28: Moving the lamp closer gives the plant brighter light, so photosynthesis speeds up and more oxygen bubbles form. A common mistake is thinking the extra heat will kill the plant; with a short move it simply gets more light.
column29: Brighter light means more energy for the plant to capture.

column9: A student counts the oxygen bubbles an elodea sprig gives off in one minute, in three trials: 24, 27, and 30 bubbles. What is the average number of bubbles per minute?
column28: Average = (24 + 27 + 30) ÷ 3 = 81 ÷ 3 = 27 bubbles per minute. A common mistake is dividing by the wrong number of trials.
column29: Add the three counts, then divide by the number of trials.

column9: Glucose has the formula C₆H₁₂O₆. How many carbon atoms are in one molecule of glucose?
column28: The subscript after C is 6, so one glucose has 6 carbon atoms (and 12 hydrogen, 6 oxygen). A common mistake is adding all the subscripts together.
column29: Look at the small number right after the C.

column9: A saguaro cactus has spines instead of flat leaves. Where does it carry out most of its photosynthesis?
column14: In its spines
column15: It can't do photosynthesis
column16: In its roots
column17: In its thick green stem
column28: A cactus stem is green because it is full of chloroplasts, so the stem does the photosynthesis. Spines are modified leaves that protect the plant and save water; they are not green. Roots are underground with no light.
column29: Photosynthesis happens wherever there is chlorophyll. Which part of a cactus is green?

column9: Kelp is a large seaweed that grows in the ocean. Where does it get the carbon dioxide it needs for photosynthesis?
column14: From the salt in the water, which breaks down into carbon dioxide
column15: From sand on the sea floor, which kelp roots pull carbon out of
column16: From carbon dioxide dissolved in the seawater
column17: From fish it eats
column28: Carbon dioxide from the air dissolves in water, and water organisms like kelp and algae absorb it. Kelp doesn't eat fish, and sand and salt don't supply carbon dioxide.
column29: Gases from the air can dissolve into water, just like the fizz in soda.

column9: An indoor farm in a warehouse grows lettuce with no windows at all. What must the farm supply so the lettuce can do photosynthesis?
column14: Grow lights
column15: Extra oxygen
column16: Sugar water
column17: Loud music
column28: Photosynthesis needs light energy, so indoor farms use grow lights in place of sunlight. Plants make their own sugar, so sugar water isn't needed, and extra oxygen is not a reactant.
column29: What does a window normally give a plant?

column9: Which of these is NOT a way a plant uses the glucose it makes?
column14: Breaking it down in cellular respiration to make ATP
column15: Releasing it into the air as a gas
column16: Storing it as starch
column17: Building cellulose for its cell walls
column28: Plants burn glucose for ATP, store it as starch, and build cellulose from it. Glucose is a solid sugar; it is not given off as a gas. The gas a plant releases from photosynthesis is oxygen.
column29: Three of these keep the sugar inside the plant. Which one doesn't make sense for a sugar?

column9: Most leaves are broad and flat. How does this shape help photosynthesis?
column14: It stops water from reaching the leaf and rotting it
column15: It holds more soil
column16: It keeps carbon dioxide out
column17: It gives a large surface to catch sunlight
column28: A broad, flat leaf has a lot of surface area facing the sun, so it can absorb more light. Plants want carbon dioxide in, not out, and leaves don't hold soil.
column29: Think about how solar panels are shaped and turned toward the sun.

column9: Phytoplankton are tiny algae floating in the ocean. Why are they so important to life on Earth?
column14: They give off carbon dioxide for the animals in the ocean to breathe
column15: Their photosynthesis produces a large share of Earth's oxygen
column16: They eat most of the fish in the ocean, which keeps fish numbers in balance
column17: They have no effect on the air
column28: Phytoplankton do photosynthesis on a huge scale and produce a large share of the oxygen in the atmosphere. They also form the base of ocean food chains. They take in carbon dioxide; they don't supply it for animals to breathe.
column29: What gas does photosynthesis add to the air?

column9: When does a garden tomato plant carry out photosynthesis?
column14: Only at night
column15: Equally all day and all night
column16: Only while light is shining on it
column17: Only in winter
column28: Photosynthesis needs light, so it happens during the day (or under grow lights). At night the plant still does cellular respiration but not photosynthesis. A common mistake is thinking plants do photosynthesis around the clock.
column29: What does photosynthesis need that is missing at night?

column9: Which is the chemical formula for glucose?
column14: O₂
column15: H₂O
column16: CO₂
column17: C₆H₁₂O₆
column28: Glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆. CO₂ is carbon dioxide, H₂O is water, and O₂ is oxygen gas; those are the other molecules in the photosynthesis equation.
column29: Glucose is the largest molecule in the photosynthesis equation.

column9: Animal cells contain chloroplasts.
column28: False. Chloroplasts are found in plant and algae cells, not animal cells. Animals must eat food. A common mistake is confusing chloroplasts with mitochondria, which both plant and animal cells have.
column29: Can a dog make its own food from sunlight?

column9: Which of these cells would contain the MOST chloroplasts?
column14: A cell from a spinach leaf
column15: A cell from a carrot root
column16: A cell from a mushroom
column17: A human skin cell
column28: Spinach leaf cells are green and packed with chloroplasts because leaves do most photosynthesis. Carrot roots grow underground, and human and mushroom cells have no chloroplasts at all.
column29: Which cell is green and gets sunlight?

column9: On a sunny day, which way do gases move through the tiny pores on the underside of a leaf during photosynthesis?
column14: Both gases move in
column15: Oxygen moves in, and carbon dioxide moves out
column16: Carbon dioxide moves in, and oxygen moves out
column17: No gases move through them
column28: In sunlight, carbon dioxide enters the leaf to be used and the oxygen made by photosynthesis leaves. The opposite direction happens mainly at night, when only cellular respiration is going on.
column29: Which gas does photosynthesis use, and which does it make?

column9: Tomato plants are planted in deep shade under a large tree. Compared with tomato plants in full sun, they will most likely...
column14: stop doing cellular respiration
column15: make less glucose and grow more slowly
column16: make the same amount of glucose
column17: make more glucose and grow faster
column28: Less light means less energy for photosynthesis, so the shaded plants make less glucose and grow more slowly. They still do cellular respiration, because every living cell needs ATP.
column29: What does shade take away from the plant?

column9: Match each part of a plant cell to what happens there.
column14: Thylakoid membranes :: Light energy is captured
column15: Stroma :: Carbon dioxide is built into sugar
column16: Mitochondria :: Glucose is broken down to make ATP
column28: Light energy is captured in the thylakoid membranes, sugar is built in the stroma (the Calvin cycle), and mitochondria break glucose down in cellular respiration. Mixing up chloroplasts and mitochondria is the most common mistake.
column29: Two of these are inside the chloroplast; one is a different organelle.

column9: On a sunny February day in Wisconsin, a white pine still has its green needles, but a sugar maple has no leaves. What can the pine do that the bare maple can't?
column14: Carry out photosynthesis
column15: Carry out cellular respiration
column16: Grow roots
column17: Absorb water
column28: The pine's needles have chlorophyll, so on mild sunny days it can do some photosynthesis. The bare maple has no leaves to capture light. Both trees still do cellular respiration all winter.
column29: Which tree still has green parts to catch the sunlight?

column9: Select every molecule the Calvin cycle needs as an input. Select all that apply.
column14: Carbon dioxide
column15: ATP
column16: NADPH
column17: Oxygen gas
column28: The Calvin cycle uses carbon dioxide plus the ATP and NADPH made in the light-dependent reactions. Oxygen is a product of the light reactions, and glucose is what the cycle makes, not what it uses.
column29: The cycle needs a source of carbon and two energy carriers.

column9: Select every product of the light-dependent reactions. Select all that apply.
column14: Oxygen gas
column15: ATP
column16: NADPH
column17: Glucose
column28: The light-dependent reactions release oxygen and make the energy carriers ATP and NADPH. Glucose is made later in the Calvin cycle, and carbon dioxide is used by the Calvin cycle, not made by the light reactions.
column29: This stage makes the energy carriers and gives off one gas. Sugar comes later.

column9: In the light-dependent reactions, molecules of ___ are split apart, and oxygen gas is released.
column28: Water is split in the thylakoids. Its electrons replace the ones chlorophyll loses, and its oxygen atoms pair up and leave as oxygen gas. A common mistake is writing carbon dioxide; the oxygen gas does not come from CO₂.
column29: This reactant comes up from the roots.

column9: The balanced equation is 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. How many water molecules are used to make 2 molecules of glucose?
column28: One glucose uses 6 water molecules, so two glucose use 2 × 6 = 12. A common mistake is answering 6 and forgetting to double.
column29: Find how many water molecules one glucose needs, then double it.

column9: In a floating leaf disk lab, 10 spinach disks sink to the bottom of a cup of baking soda solution. After 12 minutes under a lamp, 7 disks are floating. What percent of the disks are floating?
column28: Percent = 7 ÷ 10 × 100 = 70%. A common mistake is dividing 10 by 7 or using the 12 minutes.
column29: Divide the floating disks by the total disks, then multiply by 100.

column9: An elodea sprig gives off 45 oxygen bubbles in 3 minutes. What is its rate in bubbles per minute?
column28: Rate = 45 bubbles ÷ 3 minutes = 15 bubbles per minute. A common mistake is multiplying instead of dividing.
column29: "Per minute" means divide by the number of minutes.

column9: Most of the material in the wood of a large oak tree was built from atoms that came from...
column14: fertilizer added by people
column15: minerals in the soil
column16: sunlight that turned into matter
column17: carbon dioxide taken from the air
column28: Wood is mostly cellulose, made from glucose. The carbon and most of the oxygen in it came from carbon dioxide in the air. Light provides energy but does not become matter, and soil minerals make up only a tiny part of a tree's mass. Choosing the soil is the most common mistake.
column29: Wood is made of glucose chains. Which reactant brings the carbon?

column9: What is the job of NADPH in photosynthesis?
column14: It is the sugar made at the end of photosynthesis, which the plant then stores as starch
column15: It carries high-energy electrons from the light-dependent reactions to the Calvin cycle
column16: It is the green pigment that absorbs light
column17: It opens the tiny pores on the underside of the leaf to let carbon dioxide in for the Calvin cycle
column28: NADPH is an energy carrier: it picks up high-energy electrons (and hydrogen) in the thylakoids and delivers them to the Calvin cycle to build sugar. Chlorophyll is the pigment, glucose is the sugar, and guard cells open the pores.
column29: Think of NADPH as a delivery truck. What does it carry, and to where?

column9: The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH and leaves behind ADP and NADP⁺. What happens to the ADP and NADP⁺?
column14: They are destroyed, and the plant must build brand-new ones from minerals in the soil
column15: They are turned into glucose
column16: They go back to the thylakoids, where the light-dependent reactions recharge them
column17: They leave the leaf through the pores
column28: ADP and NADP⁺ are the "empty" carriers. They return to the thylakoids, where light energy recharges them into ATP and NADPH, so the two stages keep cycling. They are not built into glucose and are not lost from the leaf.
column29: Think of a rechargeable battery that goes back to the charger.

column9: A student adds baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) to the water around an elodea sprig, and the plant starts giving off more bubbles. Why?
column14: It adds dissolved carbon dioxide (as bicarbonate) that the plant uses for photosynthesis
column15: The baking soda is a sugar the plant eats
column16: The baking soda makes the light brighter
column17: The baking soda adds extra oxygen to the water, and the plant releases that oxygen as bubbles
column28: Baking soda supplies dissolved carbon dioxide (as bicarbonate), a reactant of photosynthesis. More reactant means a faster rate and more oxygen bubbles. Baking soda isn't a sugar, and plants don't eat sugar; they make it.
column29: Which reactant could a chemical in the water be supplying?

column9: In the floating leaf disk lab, disks that have sunk in baking soda solution slowly rise to the top while under a lamp. What makes them float?
column14: Carbon dioxide from cellular respiration fills the air spaces inside the disks
column15: The disks soak up the baking soda and get lighter than the water around them
column16: Water evaporates out of the disks
column17: Oxygen made by photosynthesis fills the air spaces inside the leaf disks
column28: Photosynthesis makes oxygen gas, which collects in the spaces inside the leaf tissue and makes the disks buoyant. The faster photosynthesis goes, the faster the disks float. Carbon dioxide is used up in the light, not built up.
column29: Which gas does the leaf make when the light is on?

column9: Leaf disks are placed in plain water (no baking soda) under a bright lamp. After 20 minutes, almost none of them float. What is the best explanation?
column14: Plain water is too heavy for disks to float
column15: The disks need the sugar that baking soda provides to make the oxygen gas that floats them
column16: Plain water has very little carbon dioxide, so very little photosynthesis can happen
column17: The light is too bright for the disks
column28: Baking soda provides the carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. Without it, the disks can't make much oxygen, so they stay sunk. The disks don't need sugar; they make their own. This group acts as a control.
column29: Compare this cup to the one with baking soda. Which reactant is missing?

column9: A student breathes through a straw into blue BTB until it turns yellow (BTB turns yellow when carbon dioxide is added). She puts an elodea sprig in the yellow BTB and sets it in bright light. A few hours later it is blue again. What explains the change?
column14: The elodea used up the carbon dioxide during photosynthesis
column15: The bright light bleached the yellow color out of the BTB over a few hours
column16: The elodea released carbon dioxide into the BTB during photosynthesis
column17: The elodea added sugar to the BTB
column28: In light, elodea takes carbon dioxide out of the water for photosynthesis, so the BTB goes back to blue. Releasing carbon dioxide would keep it yellow. A control tube with no plant would show that light alone doesn't change the color.
column29: BTB is yellow when there's a lot of carbon dioxide. What must have happened to the carbon dioxide?

column9: The photosynthesis rate of pond algae is measured at 10 °C, 25 °C, and 45 °C. It is highest at 25 °C and very low at 45 °C. Why is it so low at 45 °C?
column14: Warm water holds extra carbon dioxide, so the algae get too much
column15: The high heat damages the enzymes that run photosynthesis
column16: The algae fall asleep in warm water
column17: There is too much light at 45 °C
column28: Photosynthesis (especially the Calvin cycle) is run by enzymes. Moderate warmth speeds them up, but too much heat changes their shape and they stop working. Temperature doesn't change the light, and warm water actually holds less carbon dioxide, not more.
column29: Photosynthesis is a set of chemical reactions controlled by proteins. What does too much heat do to proteins?

column9: Why is the Calvin cycle sometimes called the "light-independent reactions"?
column14: It happens only at night
column15: It makes its own light
column16: It happens in the roots, where there is no light, using the sugar the leaves send down to them
column17: It doesn't absorb light itself; it runs on ATP and NADPH made by the light-dependent reactions
column28: The Calvin cycle doesn't absorb light itself, but it runs on ATP and NADPH from the light reactions, so in a real plant it happens mostly during the day. Thinking it happens only at night ("dark reactions") is a common mistake.
column29: "Independent" here means it doesn't use light itself. What does it use instead?

column9: A pigment molecule in a thylakoid membrane absorbs light. What happens to that energy?
column14: It is turned directly into carbon dioxide molecules, which the Calvin cycle then uses to build sugar
column15: It boosts electrons to a higher energy level, and they are passed along to make ATP and NADPH
column16: It is turned back into green light
column17: It is stored as heat in the roots
column28: Absorbed light energy excites electrons in the pigment. Those high-energy electrons move along the thylakoid membrane, and their energy is used to make ATP and NADPH. Light energy is not turned into matter like carbon dioxide.
column29: Light energy has to be captured in something the Calvin cycle can use.

column9: A greenhouse owner wants LED grow lights that give the most photosynthesis for the least electricity. Which choice is best?
column14: Yellow LEDs only
column15: Green LEDs only
column16: Red and blue LEDs
column17: Green and yellow LEDs
column28: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light the most, so red and blue LEDs give the most photosynthesis per watt. Green and yellow light are absorbed the least, so much of that energy is wasted. That's why many grow lights glow purple-pink.
column29: Which colors does chlorophyll absorb best, not reflect?

column9: Leaves contain chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, and carotenoids. How does having several pigments help a plant?
column14: Extra pigments keep carbon dioxide out of the leaf so that it can't damage the chlorophyll
column15: Only one pigment works; the others are waste
column16: Extra pigments make the leaf heavier
column17: Each pigment absorbs a different range of colors, so the plant captures more of the light
column28: Each pigment absorbs best at different colors, so together they capture a wider range of light energy. Carotenoids also help protect chlorophyll from too much light. Pigments have nothing to do with keeping carbon dioxide out.
column29: Think of several nets with different-sized holes catching more kinds of fish.

column9: One geranium sits in a dark closet and another sits in a sunny window for two days. A leaf from each is boiled and tested with iodine, which turns blue-black where starch is present. What results are expected?
column14: The sunny leaf turns blue-black; the dark leaf stays orange-brown
column15: Neither leaf changes color
column16: Both leaves turn blue-black
column17: Only the dark leaf turns blue-black, because it saved its starch instead of using it
column28: The sunny plant made glucose by photosynthesis and stored the extra as starch, so iodine turns blue-black. The plant in the dark used up its stored starch in respiration and couldn't make more. Thinking the dark plant still stores starch is a common mistake.
column29: Which plant could make new sugar to store?

column9: Match each molecule to its role in photosynthesis.
column14: Carbon dioxide :: Supplies the carbon atoms used to build sugar
column15: Water :: Is taken up by the roots and used in the light-dependent reactions
column16: Glucose :: Stores chemical energy the plant can use later
column17: Oxygen :: Is given off into the air as a by-product
column28: Carbon dioxide brings the carbon, water is used in the light reactions, glucose stores the energy, and oxygen is the by-product. A common mistake is thinking oxygen is the main goal of photosynthesis; the plant is making sugar, and oxygen is left over.
column29: Start with the molecule that has carbon in it, then the one that comes from the roots.

column9: Put the steps of the floating leaf disk lab in order.
column14: Place the cup under a lamp
column15: Punch out disks from a spinach leaf
column16: Count the floating disks every minute
column17: Pull the air out of the disks with a syringe so they fill with baking soda solution and sink
column28: Punch the disks → remove the air so they fill with solution and sink → put them under the light → count floating disks over time. A common mistake is putting them under the lamp before they have sunk, which means there is nothing to measure.
column29: The disks have to sink before you can watch them rise.

column9: On a hot, dry afternoon, a corn plant closes the tiny pores in its leaves to save water. Why does its photosynthesis slow down?
column14: The roots stop absorbing glucose
column15: Too much water rushes into the leaf
column16: Less carbon dioxide can get into the leaf
column17: The leaves receive less light
column28: The pores are where carbon dioxide enters. When they close, carbon dioxide runs low inside the leaf and the Calvin cycle slows. The light is still there, and roots don't absorb glucose.
column29: What normally comes in through those pores?

column9: Why do plant cells need both chloroplasts and mitochondria?
column14: Chloroplasts and mitochondria do exactly the same job
column15: Chloroplasts make glucose, and mitochondria break it down to make ATP for the cell
column16: Mitochondria make glucose, and chloroplasts break it down to make ATP for the cell
column17: Mitochondria are only used when the plant is in the dark and can't do photosynthesis
column28: Chloroplasts store light energy in glucose. Mitochondria release that energy into ATP, which powers cell work. Plant mitochondria work day and night, not just in the dark.
column29: One organelle builds the fuel; the other burns it.

column9: In a Wisconsin cornfield in July, the carbon dioxide level in the air just above the plants is lower at noon than at midnight. What best explains this?
column14: During the day, photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide faster than respiration adds it
column15: Carbon dioxide sinks down into the soil at noon, when the air is warmest
column16: Corn gives off more carbon dioxide at noon, when it is doing the most photosynthesis of the day
column17: Corn does no cellular respiration at night
column28: At noon the corn is using carbon dioxide for photosynthesis faster than respiration releases it, so the level drops. At night there is only respiration, so carbon dioxide builds back up. Corn respires both day and night.
column29: Which process uses carbon dioxide, and when can it happen?

column9: Inside a chloroplast, thylakoids are stacked into grana. How does this stacking help photosynthesis?
column14: It keeps light from reaching the stroma so the sugar made there isn't damaged
column15: It lets carbon dioxide out of the chloroplast faster so it doesn't build up
column16: It stores starch for winter
column17: It packs a large amount of pigment-holding membrane into a small space
column28: The thylakoid membranes hold the pigments and proteins of the light reactions. Stacking lots of them gives a huge surface for capturing light in a tiny space, like stacking solar panels.
column29: The light reactions happen on membranes. More membrane means...

column9: Where is the energy stored in a glucose molecule made by photosynthesis?
column14: In the heat around it
column15: In the chemical bonds between its atoms
column16: In its color
column17: In its magnetism
column28: Photosynthesis stores light energy as chemical energy in the bonds of glucose. Cellular respiration later breaks those bonds and moves the energy into ATP. Glucose is colorless, so the energy isn't in its color.
column29: Chemical energy is held in the connections between atoms.

column9: A spider plant sits in a dim corner of a 22 °C room. Which changes would most likely increase its rate of photosynthesis? Select all that apply.
column14: Move it to a sunny window
column15: Put a grow light above it
column16: Move it into a dark closet
column17: Heat the room to 50 °C
column18: Cover its leaves with a layer of dust
column28: In a dim corner, light is what limits the plant, so more light (a sunny window or a grow light) speeds up photosynthesis. A dark closet or dusty leaves block light, and 50 °C is hot enough to damage the plant's enzymes.
column29: What is the plant short on in a dim corner?

column9: Which of these observations are evidence that photosynthesis is happening? Select all that apply.
column14: Bubbles of gas rise from an elodea sprig under a lamp
column15: Leaf disks in baking soda solution float up under a lamp
column16: Yellow BTB around a water plant in the light turns blue
column17: A potted plant's leaves droop after a week without water
column18: Iodine on a leaf kept in the dark shows no starch
column28: Oxygen bubbles, floating leaf disks (filled with oxygen), and BTB turning blue (carbon dioxide used) all show photosynthesis making oxygen or using carbon dioxide. Drooping leaves show water loss, and no starch in a dark-kept leaf shows photosynthesis was NOT happening.
column29: Look for signs that oxygen is being made or carbon dioxide is being used up.

column9: Seaweeds grow in shallow ocean water but are not found on the dark sea floor thousands of meters down. Why?
column14: Fish eat all the seaweed in deep water
column15: Deep water is too salty
column16: Sunlight can't reach that deep, so seaweeds couldn't do photosynthesis there
column17: There is no carbon dioxide in deep water, because it all stays near the surface
column28: Sunlight fades quickly with depth, and below about 200 meters there is too little light for photosynthesis. Deep water is not saltier, and it still contains dissolved carbon dioxide.
column29: What does photosynthesis need that fades away as you go deeper?

column9: A farmer pumps extra carbon dioxide into a bright, warm greenhouse, and the tomato plants grow faster. Why?
column14: Carbon dioxide is a reactant, so with plenty of light the plants make more glucose
column15: Carbon dioxide gives the plants more light
column16: The plants breathe the carbon dioxide instead of oxygen
column17: Carbon dioxide acts as a fertilizer that adds nitrogen and other minerals to the soil
column28: In bright, warm conditions, carbon dioxide is often the limiting factor. Adding more lets the Calvin cycle build sugar faster, so the plants grow faster. Carbon dioxide doesn't add light or soil minerals.
column29: Which side of the photosynthesis equation is carbon dioxide on?

column9: Which statement best explains how photosynthesis follows the law of conservation of matter?
column14: Light energy turns into the carbon atoms that make up glucose, so the plant gains new matter
column15: Some of the oxygen atoms disappear when the oxygen gas leaves the leaf
column16: The plant creates new carbon atoms as it grows
column17: Atoms in CO₂ and water are rearranged into glucose and O₂; none are created or destroyed
column28: Photosynthesis rearranges atoms: every carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atom in the products came from carbon dioxide and water. Light supplies energy but never becomes atoms. Thinking sunlight becomes the plant's mass is a common mistake.
column29: Count atoms on both sides of a balanced equation. Where did every atom in glucose come from?

column9: Elodea bubbles per minute were counted with different amounts of baking soda in the water: 0 g gave 2, 0.1 g gave 8, 0.2 g gave 14, and 0.4 g gave 15. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: The rate kept rising by the same amount with every addition of baking soda, with no limit
column15: Baking soda slowed photosynthesis
column16: More baking soda increased the rate up to about 0.2 g, and then the rate leveled off
column17: Baking soda had no effect on the rate
column28: From 0 to 0.2 g the rate jumped from 2 to 14, but doubling to 0.4 g added only 1 more bubble. Something else, likely light, became the limiting factor. A common mistake is assuming the trend continues forever without looking at the last data point.
column29: Compare the jump from 0.1 to 0.2 g with the jump from 0.2 to 0.4 g.

column9: Scientists give a plant water made with a heavy, traceable form of oxygen (oxygen-18). The carbon dioxide it gets is normal. Where will most of the traceable oxygen show up first?
column14: In the oxygen gas the plant releases
column15: In the carbon dioxide the plant releases
column16: In the soil around the roots
column17: In the glucose the plant makes
column28: Water is split in the light-dependent reactions, and its oxygen atoms leave as oxygen gas, so the tracer shows up in the O₂. Scientists did this experiment in 1941. Assuming the tracer ends up in glucose is a common mistake.
column29: Which molecule gets split apart in the light-dependent reactions, and what gas is released when it is?

column9: A plant is given normal water, but the carbon dioxide it takes in is made with a heavy, traceable form of oxygen (oxygen-18). Where will that traceable oxygen end up?
column14: In the chlorophyll
column15: In the glucose the plant makes
column16: In the ATP
column17: In the oxygen gas the plant releases
column28: Carbon dioxide's atoms are built into sugar in the Calvin cycle, so its oxygen ends up in glucose, not in the oxygen gas. The released oxygen gas comes from water. Thinking the oxygen gas comes from carbon dioxide is the most common photosynthesis misconception.
column29: Carbon dioxide enters the Calvin cycle. What does the Calvin cycle make?

column9: Using 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, how many carbon dioxide molecules does a plant need to make 3 molecules of glucose?
column28: Each glucose needs 6 CO₂ (one for each of its 6 carbon atoms), so 3 glucose need 3 × 6 = 18 CO₂. A common mistake is answering 6 or adding 6 + 3.
column29: How many CO₂ molecules does one glucose need? Then multiply.

column9: Count the oxygen atoms on the reactant side of 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. How many are there in total?
column28: 6CO₂ has 6 × 2 = 12 oxygen atoms and 6H₂O has 6 × 1 = 6, so 12 + 6 = 18. The product side also has 6 + 12 = 18, so it balances. A common mistake is forgetting to multiply the subscript by the coefficient.
column29: Multiply each coefficient by the number of oxygen atoms in that molecule, then add.

column9: Put these events of photosynthesis in order, starting with sunlight hitting a leaf.
column14: Energy-carrying molecules are charged up in the thylakoids
column15: Carbon dioxide is built into sugar in the stroma
column16: Light energy is absorbed by pigments in the thylakoid membranes
column17: The charged carriers bring their energy to the stroma
column18: The sugar is stored as starch or broken down in cellular respiration
column28: Light is absorbed → energy carriers (ATP and NADPH) are charged → they bring the energy to the stroma → carbon dioxide is built into sugar → the sugar is stored or used. A common mistake is putting sugar-building first, but the Calvin cycle can't run until the carriers are charged.
column29: Energy has to be captured before it can be delivered, and delivered before it can be used.

column9: Follow one carbon atom from the air into a potato. Put the steps in order.
column14: The carbon atom is built into a sugar molecule in the stroma
column15: The sugar travels down the stem to the potato and is stored as starch
column16: The carbon atom is part of a carbon dioxide molecule in the air
column17: The carbon dioxide diffuses into a chloroplast in a leaf cell
column18: The carbon dioxide enters the leaf through a tiny pore on its underside
column28: Air → through a leaf pore → into a chloroplast → built into sugar in the Calvin cycle → moved to the potato and stored as starch. A common mistake is thinking the carbon in a potato came from the soil around it.
column29: The atom has to get inside the leaf, then inside the chloroplast, before it can become sugar.

column9: On the same maple tree, leaves at the shady bottom of the tree have more chlorophyll per cell than leaves at the sunny top. How does this help the shaded leaves?
column14: It lets them use less carbon dioxide
column15: It lets them do photosynthesis at night, when there is no sunlight at all
column16: It keeps them from doing cellular respiration, so they save their sugar
column17: It lets them capture more of the dim light that reaches them
column28: Shaded leaves get less light, so having more light-absorbing pigment helps them catch as much of it as possible. More chlorophyll doesn't let a leaf work at night, and every leaf cell still does cellular respiration.
column29: What is a shaded leaf short on, and what does chlorophyll do?

column9: Scientists dissolve the green pigment out of spinach leaves into a test tube. When light shines on it, the pigment absorbs light, but no oxygen or sugar is made. What is the best explanation?
column14: Spinach can't do photosynthesis
column15: Photosynthesis needs the whole chloroplast, with its membranes and enzymes, not just the pigment
column16: Oxygen and sugar are both made, but they are invisible and dissolve right away inside the test tube
column17: The pigment is not really able to absorb light
column28: The pigment captures light, but the energy carriers, thylakoid membranes, water-splitting proteins, and Calvin cycle enzymes are needed to turn that energy into oxygen and sugar. The test tube shows the pigment does absorb light, so the problem is the missing machinery.
column29: Photosynthesis has many parts working together. What was left behind when only the pigment was removed?

column9: A student wants to test whether light color affects photosynthesis in elodea, using red, green, and blue lamps. Which plan makes it a fair test?
column14: Put each lamp at a different distance from the elodea so that all three colors look equally bright
column15: Use a bigger elodea sprig under the green lamp to make up for it
column16: Keep lamp brightness, lamp distance, water temperature, and baking soda the same for every color
column17: Use a different kind of water plant for each color
column28: Only the light color should change. Brightness, distance, temperature, carbon dioxide, and plant type must stay constant so any difference in bubbles is caused by color. Changing the plant size or distance adds a second variable.
column29: In a fair test, how many things should change?

column9: Elodea gave off 3 bubbles per minute under green light, 18 under red light, and 15 under blue light, with all other conditions the same. Which conclusion is best supported?
column14: Elodea doesn't need light to do photosynthesis
column15: Red light adds carbon dioxide to the water
column16: Green light is the best color for photosynthesis, since plants are green
column17: Elodea's pigments absorb red and blue light better than green light
column28: Red and blue light gave the fastest rates, which shows they are absorbed and used much more than green. Green gave the slowest rate because the pigments reflect most green light. Green being the plant's color does not make it the best light.
column29: More bubbles means more photosynthesis. Which colors gave the most?

column9: Three sealed tubes start with green BTB. Tube 1 has elodea in the light and turns blue. Tube 2 has elodea in the dark and turns yellow. Tube 3 has no plant, sits in the light, and stays green. What does Tube 3 show?
column14: Light alone doesn't change BTB, so the plant caused the color changes in Tubes 1 and 2
column15: Tube 3 is the experimental group, the one that tests how light affects the elodea plant
column16: BTB can't change color
column17: Elodea does photosynthesis in the dark
column28: Tube 3 is the control. Because it stayed green in the light, light by itself didn't change the BTB. That means the plant's photosynthesis (using CO₂, turning blue) and respiration (adding CO₂, turning yellow) caused the changes. Calling the control an experimental group is a common mistake.
column29: What is different about Tube 3 compared with Tube 1?

column9: In a lab, scientists give the fluid from inside chloroplasts (the stroma) carbon dioxide, ATP, and NADPH, and keep it in total darkness. Will sugar be made?
column14: Yes, but only oxygen will be made, not sugar
column15: No, because the Calvin cycle needs the oxygen gas made by the light-dependent reactions
column16: Yes, because the Calvin cycle doesn't use light directly if it has ATP and NADPH
column17: No, because the Calvin cycle absorbs light itself
column28: The Calvin cycle runs on ATP and NADPH; light is only needed to make those carriers in the thylakoids. If they are supplied directly, sugar can be made in the dark. Thinking the Calvin cycle absorbs light itself is a common mistake.
column29: What does the Calvin cycle actually use up? Is light on that list?

column9: A chemical blocks the light-dependent reactions in a plant, but the plant still has plenty of carbon dioxide. What happens to the Calvin cycle soon after?
column14: It keeps going normally because it doesn't need light
column15: It slows and stops because it runs out of ATP and NADPH
column16: It starts releasing oxygen instead
column17: It speeds up because it has more carbon dioxide to use
column28: The Calvin cycle depends on the ATP and NADPH made by the light reactions. Once the light reactions are blocked, the supply runs out and sugar-building stops. "Doesn't use light directly" doesn't mean it can run on its own.
column29: The Calvin cycle needs two energy carriers. Where do they come from?

column9: A healthy, living plant is sealed in a glass jar under very dim light. The carbon dioxide level in the jar stays the same all day. What is the best explanation?
column14: Photosynthesis is using carbon dioxide as fast as cellular respiration releases it
column15: The plant is doing neither photosynthesis nor respiration, because the light is too dim
column16: Carbon dioxide can't change inside a sealed jar
column17: The plant has stopped all of its chemical reactions
column28: A living plant always does cellular respiration, which adds carbon dioxide. In dim light, photosynthesis can be just fast enough to use up exactly that much, so the level stays flat. Thinking "no change" means "nothing is happening" is a common mistake; living cells never stop respiring.
column29: Two processes are happening in the leaf. One adds carbon dioxide and one removes it.

column9: A student says, "Plants get their food from the soil. That's why we add fertilizer." Which response best corrects the student?
column14: The student is right; fertilizer is plant food that gives plants all the energy they need to grow tall
column15: Plants don't need food at all
column16: Plants get their food from the water, not the soil
column17: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis; fertilizer gives minerals like nitrogen, not food energy
column28: Plants are autotrophs that make glucose by photosynthesis. Fertilizer provides minerals such as nitrogen and phosphorus that plants use to build proteins and DNA, but it provides no food energy. Calling fertilizer "plant food" is the source of the misconception.
column29: Where does a plant's energy come from, and what are minerals used for?

column9: Two plants are kept in dim light. One gets normal air and one gets air with double the carbon dioxide. Both make almost the same amount of sugar. What is the best explanation?
column14: Carbon dioxide is not a reactant in photosynthesis
column15: In dim light, light is the limiting factor, so extra carbon dioxide doesn't help much
column16: The plants can't take in any carbon dioxide in dim light, so neither plant used any of it at all
column17: Extra carbon dioxide always stops photosynthesis
column28: The rate is held back by whichever factor is in shortest supply. Here, light is too low, so the plants can't use the extra carbon dioxide. In bright light, the extra carbon dioxide would speed them up. Thinking more of any reactant always speeds the reaction is a common mistake.
column29: If one ingredient is running short, does adding more of a different ingredient help?

column9: An elodea sprig in a test tube is making very few bubbles. Select every change that would most likely increase its bubbles per minute. Select all that apply.
column14: Move the lamp closer
column15: Add a pinch of baking soda to the water
column16: Put the tube in a dark cabinet
column17: Put the tube in ice water
column19: Wrap the tube in black paper
column28: More light (lamp closer), more carbon dioxide (baking soda), and warmer water up to a moderate temperature all speed up photosynthesis. Darkness and black paper block light, and ice water slows the enzymes.
column29: Think about the three main factors: light, carbon dioxide, and temperature.

column9: A student writes the photosynthesis equation as 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂. What is wrong with it?
column14: Hydrogen isn't balanced; it should be 12H₂O
column15: Carbon isn't balanced; it should be 12CO₂
column16: Oxygen isn't balanced; it should be 6O₂ on the product side
column17: Nothing is wrong; it is balanced
column28: Carbon (6 = 6) and hydrogen (12 = 12) balance, but oxygen does not: the left has 12 + 6 = 18, and the right has only 6 + 2 = 8. Changing O₂ to 6O₂ gives 6 + 12 = 18. A common mistake is checking only carbon.
column29: Count each kind of atom on both sides. Which one doesn't match?

column9: A plant in bright light is suddenly given air with no carbon dioxide at all. What happens to its release of oxygen over the next while?
column14: It slows and stops, because the stalled Calvin cycle no longer returns ADP and NADP⁺ to be recharged
column15: It keeps going at the same rate forever, because carbon dioxide isn't used by the light reactions at all
column16: The plant starts turning oxygen into carbon dioxide to replace it
column17: It speeds up because the plant has nothing else to do
column28: The light reactions need empty carriers (ADP and NADP⁺) to fill. Without carbon dioxide, the Calvin cycle stops using ATP and NADPH, so no empty carriers come back, and the light reactions (and oxygen release) shut down. The stages depend on each other in both directions.
column29: The two stages pass energy carriers back and forth. What happens if one side stops sending them back?

column9: Four cups of sunk leaf disks are set up. Select every cup where the disks are expected to float within 20 minutes. Select all that apply.
column14: Baking soda solution under a bright white lamp
column15: Baking soda solution sealed inside a dark box
column16: Disks that were boiled first (cells killed), in baking soda solution under a bright lamp
column17: Baking soda solution under a bright red LED
column28: Floating needs living cells, light, and carbon dioxide. White light and red light both drive photosynthesis (red is absorbed well), so those disks fill with oxygen and float. The dark box has no light, and boiled disks have dead cells that can't photosynthesize.
column29: For each cup, ask: living cells? light? carbon dioxide?

column9: In a snowy Wisconsin winter, thick ice covered by deep snow can cause "winterkill," where fish in a lake die from low oxygen. Which explanation is best?
column14: Algae give off carbon dioxide only in the winter, and that carbon dioxide pushes the oxygen out of the lake
column15: Cold water can't hold any oxygen at all
column16: The fish stop doing cellular respiration in winter
column17: Snow blocks the light, so photosynthesis under the ice stops while respiration keeps using oxygen
column28: Ice keeps new oxygen from the air out, and snow blocks the light, so photosynthesis under the ice stops. Fish, plants, and decomposers keep using oxygen in respiration, so it runs out. Cold water actually holds more oxygen than warm water, and fish still respire in winter.
column29: Which process adds oxygen to the lake, and what does it need that snow takes away?

column9: Match each situation to the factor that is most likely limiting photosynthesis.
column14: A fern on the shady floor of a thick forest :: Light
column15: A sunny greenhouse sealed with no fresh air for several days :: Carbon dioxide
column16: Pond plants in near-freezing water on a sunny day :: Temperature
column17: A sunny garden plant in soil that hasn't been watered for weeks :: Water
column28: The shaded fern lacks light, the sealed greenhouse has used up its carbon dioxide, the cold pond slows enzymes, and the dry soil leaves too little water. Find what each situation is short on while it has plenty of everything else.
column29: For each one, ask which ingredient or condition is in short supply.

column9: Students claim, "More light always means more photosynthesis." Their elodea data: 1,000 lux gave 10 bubbles/min, 2,000 lux gave 20, 4,000 lux gave 26, and 8,000 lux gave 26. Which evaluation of the claim is best?
column14: The claim is fully supported because 8,000 lux gave the most bubbles
column15: The claim is wrong because light had no effect
column16: The claim is only partly supported: the rate rose up to about 4,000 lux, then leveled off
column17: The claim is fully supported because the rate never went down, even at the brightest light
column28: The rate doubled from 1,000 to 2,000 lux and rose again at 4,000 lux, but doubling to 8,000 lux changed nothing. Past that point another factor, like carbon dioxide or temperature, was limiting. "Didn't go down" is not the same as "always goes up."
column29: Look at what happened when the light was doubled the last time.
